shippingNews.postTitle: Gaia Desgagnes Makes Unusual Trip to Lake Superior

stories.body: Tanker Gaia Desgagnes headed for the Soo Locks Monday morning. [Roger LeLievre] The Canadian-flagged Tanker Gaia Desgagnes was upbound at the Soo Locks late Monday morning headed for Thunder Bay, ON, with a cargo of diesel. This is a rare trip for the 2018-built vessel, which is owned by Groupe Desgagnes, Quebec City.

shippingNews.postTitle: Duluth Ship Fans Welcome Visiting R/V Neil Armstrong

stories.body: DULUTH, MN – The R/V Neil Armstrong arrived at Duluth Monday morning from its home port of Woods Hole, MA. The University of Minnesota Duluth is working with the research vessel to detect and observe neutrino interactions in Lake Superior. Neutrinos are the most abundant particles that have mass in the universe, and they pass through everything. They are very difficult to detect, so studying them requires special instruments. todayInHistory.title: Life Aboard the Edmund Fitzgerald Described in Letters from Cadet
todayInHistory.text: David "Cowboy" Weiss in 1974. [GLSHS] DETROIT, MI – It wasn't just the hat that earned Edmund Fitzgerald crew member David Weiss his nickname "Cowboy." It was his friend and Great Lakes Maritime Academy classmate David James, who had just watched Frank Zappa's 1971 movie "200 Motels" featuring the character Lonesome Cowboy Burt. When James saw Weiss standing outside a classroom dressed in black and wearing a cowboy hat, the nickname came easily."He looked a little different," James said. Weiss was less "bummy" than the rest of their classmates, who dressed to emulate the sailors they were training to join. The day they met, James gave Weiss his nickname "Cowboy Burt." DuMouchelles auction house in downtown Detroit is selling letters written by a man killed in the Edmund Fitzgerald sinking in Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975. The letters were written by David Weiss while he was on the Fitzgerald. The friendship between Weiss and James is chronicled in a series of letters they exchanged while out on the inland seas in 1975, when Weiss was on the Edmund Fitzgerald and James on the Walter A. Sterling. The last was sent Oct. 30, about two weeks before Weiss went down with the Edmund Fitzgerald during a storm in Lake Superior. Twenty-eight crewmates perished along with him. todayInHistory.title: Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest to Speak In Ludington
todayInHistory.text: LUDINGTON, MI – Maritime historian, author and shipwreck explorer Valerie van Heest, whose work has helped shape the visitor experience at all three Mason County Historical Society museums, will be the featured speaker at the society’s annual dinner meeting Thursday, Dec. 3. Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest. [Mason County Historical Society] Van Heest, one of Michigan’s leading maritime historians and shipwreck researchers, will present “History of the Great Lakes,” based on her new book, “A History of the Great Lakes in Twelve Shipwrecks.” The program will explore 250 years of Great Lakes history through a dozen shipwrecks, showing how these underwater discoveries reveal broader stories of conflict, settlement, innovation and change. The annual meeting will take place at the United Methodist Church of Ludington, 5810 Bryant Road. Doors will open at 5:45 p.m., with dinner beginning at 6 p.m. The society’s annual business meeting and organizational updates will follow dinner, and van Heest’s presentation will begin at 7:30 p.m. Van Heest is co-founder and president of the Michigan Shipwreck Research Association and has helped discover about 20 shipwrecks off Michigan’s west coast while participating in archaeological investigations at more than 50 shipwreck sites throughout the Great Lakes. Her work combines archival research with underwater exploration, including side-scan sonar surveys, remotely operated vehicles and archaeological documentation. She has also spent years

marineWeather.synopsis: A 29.5 inch low over Delaware this morning deepens to 29.4 inches as it moves offshore near Cape Cod Friday morning and then to Newfoundland by Saturday morning. Meanwhile, 30.4 inch high pressure over northern Manitoba gradually weakens to 30.3 inches over northwest Ontario by Friday and expands southward to the Ozarks by Saturday morning. High pressure slowly shifts eastward to the Upper Great Lakes at 30.3 inches by Saturday and encompasses much of the eastern CONUS while strengthening to 30.5 inches by Monday.

29.5 inch low pressure will advance into the northeastern United States today. Progression of the low will support continued increases in northerly winds, with gusts exceeding gale force through this evening as 30.4 inch high pressure builds into the Canadian Great Plains. A Gale Warning remains in effect until 9 PM CST this evening over the southern two-thirds of the waters. Northerly winds will remain steadily breezy---though below gale thresholds---through the day on Friday as the aforementioned high nudges east toward the Hudson Bay. Winds will taper Sunday into Monday as 30.2 inch high pressure builds directly over the open waters. Persistent northerly winds will allow for continued lake effect precipitation through Friday. Expecting precip to gradually drift eastward tonight into Friday. Low level temperatures will be supportive for mainly rain, though some snow could mix in over the northern half of the lake. A few thunderstorms are possible, particularly over the southern half of the waters. Can't rule out a waterspout in any deeper thunderstorms that manage to develop. marineWeather.synopsis: Low pressure, 29.50 inches, travels east across the Ohio Valley today. This will reinforce northeast to north flow across the Great Lakes, allowing winds to rapidly increase this morning and through tomorrow. Numerous to widespread lake effect rain showers will also be likely to end the week.

Low pressure 29.60 inches tracking across the Ohio Valley early this morning will exit to off the Mid Atlantic coast today as a sharp trough averaging 29.80 inches lingers across the lake through this afternoon. Weaker troughing averaging 30.00 inches then persists for Friday and the weekend. High pressure 30.40 inches builds over the lake early next week.

A 29.5 inch low over the Ohio Valley will give way to a secondary low just off the Delmarva this afternoon. This 29.3 inch coastal low will move northeast and offshore of the New England coast tonight through Friday night before moving into the Canadian Maritimes Saturday while deepening to 29.1 inches. A 30.4 inch high will then build from the upper Mississippi Valley Sunday to the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley Monday. This high will become nearly stationary over the Ohio Valley and Mid Atlantic through at least the middle of next week.
